definition: Explanation-based learning (EBL) is a form of machine learning that exploits a very strong, or even perfect, domain theory (i.e.
details: a formal theory of an application domain akin to a domain model in ontology engineering, not to be confused with Scott's domain theory) in order to make generalizations or form concepts from training examples. It is also linked with Encoding (memory) to help with Learning.

explainer.lead: Explanation-based learning turns a single training example into a reusable rule by explaining that example with a detailed theory of the domain. It matters when reliable background knowledge is available and learning from many examples alone would be inefficient.

tiers.eli5: Imagine learning why one toy can be picked up: you already know that small, light things with handles are easy to grasp. Instead of testing hundreds of toys, you use that knowledge to explain one success and make a general rule for next time.
tiers.practitioner: Apply EBL when the application has a strong formal domain theory and training examples whose outcomes can be derived from that theory. The learned generalization is only as dependable as the theory and the explanation, so incomplete or incorrect domain knowledge is a central pitfall.
tiers.paperLevel: Given a domain theory T, a training example, and a target concept, EBL constructs an explanation showing how T accounts for the example, then generalizes that explanation into a concept definition or rule. With a perfect domain theory, the generalization inherits the theory's deductive basis rather than relying solely on statistical regularities across examples; imperfect theories undermine that guarantee.

explainer.example: Suppose a domain theory says that an object is liftable when it is both light and graspable. A training example shows a particular light cup with a handle being lifted; EBL explains the success using those properties and generalizes it to other light, graspable objects rather than only that cup.
explainer.intuition: Instead of noticing patterns across many examples, EBL asks why one example works and uses existing domain knowledge to answer. That explanation supplies the structure for a broader, reusable generalization.
howItWorks: Start with a strong formal theory describing the application domain.
Provide a training example and the concept or outcome to be learned.
Use the domain theory to explain why the example has that outcome.
Generalize the explanation beyond the example's specific details.
Retain the result as a generalized concept or rule.
explainer.whyItMatters: EBL shows how prior knowledge can reduce dependence on large collections of training examples. It also connects concept formation with reasoning, producing generalizations grounded in an explicit explanation.
misconceptions: EBL is not simply learning a statistical pattern from many examples; it reasons from a domain theory.
Its domain theory means a formal theory of an application domain, not Scott's domain theory.
A strong or perfect theory does not make every real-world domain theory reliable; errors in the theory affect learned generalizations.
